groups: Where a protest may be held
Complaining about force used by police

rights.title: Right to protest
rights.point: Every citizen has a right to speak out and to gather with others peacefully and without weapons.
rights.law: Constitution of India, Article 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b)
rights.quote: (1) All citizens shall have the right— (a) to freedom of speech and expression; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms;

rights.title: Limits on that right
rights.point: The government can put reasonable limits on gatherings by law, for public order or the sovereignty and integrity of India, but only reasonable ones.
rights.law: Constitution of India, Article 19(3) (assembly); Article 19(2) (speech)
rights.quote: (3) Nothing in sub-clause (b) of the said clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order, reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause.

rights.title: Peaceful protest is a basic feature of democracy
rights.point: The Supreme Court has said that peaceful protest is part of democracy and the government should respect it.
rights.law: In re Ramlila Maidan Incident v. Home Secretary, Supreme Court, 23 February 2012, para 200 (Swatanter Kumar J.)
rights.quote: Freedom of speech, right to assemble and demonstrate by holding dharnas and peaceful agitations are the basic features of a democratic system. The people of a democratic country like ours have a right to raise their voice against the decisions and actions of the Government or even to express their resentment over the actions of the Government on any subject of social or national importance. The Government has to respect and, in fact, encourage exercise of such rights.

rights.title: Prohibitory orders: who and how long
rights.point: A District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or a specially empowered Executive Magistrate can issue a written order banning certain acts in an area. It lasts at most two months, unless the State Government extends it by up to six months more.
rights.law: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, section 163(1), (3), (4) (replaces CrPC section 144)
rights.quote: No order under this section shall remain in force for more than two months from the making thereof: Provided that if the State Government considers it necessary so to do for preventing danger to human life, health or safety or for preventing a riot or any affray, it may, by notification, direct that an order made by a Magistrate under this section shall remain in force for such further period not exceeding six months

rights.title: Prohibitory orders: you can ask for one to be cancelled
rights.point: Anyone affected can ask the Magistrate (or the State Government, for an extension) to cancel or change the order, and must be given a chance to be heard.
rights.law: BNSS 2023, section 163(5), (6) and (7)
rights.quote: Any Magistrate may, either on his own motion or on the application of any person aggrieved, rescind or alter any order made under this section

rights.title: Disobeying a prohibitory order
rights.point: Knowingly disobeying a lawful prohibitory order is an offence if it obstructs, annoys or injures, or risks injuring, anyone lawfully employed. The punishment is up to six months' simple imprisonment or a fine of up to Rs 2,500. If the disobedience causes or tends to cause danger to life, health or safety, or a riot or affray, it is up to one year or a fine of up to Rs 5,000. It is enough to know of the order, and no intent to cause harm is needed.
rights.law: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, section 223 (replaces IPC section 188)
rights.quote: Whoever, knowing that, by an order promulgated by a public servant lawfully empowered to promulgate such order, he is directed to abstain from a certain act, ... disobeys such direction,–– (a) shall, if such disobedience causes or tends to cause obstruction, annoyance or injury, ... be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to two thousand and five hundred rupees, or with both;

rights.title: Supreme Court tests for prohibitory orders
rights.point: The Supreme Court has said these orders are for emergencies, cannot be used to suppress legitimate protest, must state the facts behind them, must use the least restrictive measure, and cannot be repeated again and again.
rights.law: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, Supreme Court, 10 January 2020, para 140 (AIR 2020 SC 1308; (2020) 3 SCC 637)
rights.quote: i. ... However, the danger contemplated should be in the nature of an “emergency” and for the purpose of preventing obstruction and annoyance or injury to any person lawfully employed. ii. The power under Section 144, Cr.P.C cannot be used to suppress legitimate expression of opinion or grievance or exercise of any democratic rights. iii. An order passed under Section 144, Cr.P.C. should state the material facts to enable judicial review of the same. ... iv. While exercising the power under Section 144, Cr.P.C. the Magistrate is duty bound to balance the rights and restrictions based on the principles of proportionality and thereafter apply the least intrusive measure. v. Repetitive orders under Section 144, Cr.P.C. would be an abuse of power.

rights.title: Emergencies only
rights.point: The Court has also said such orders apply only in emergencies, though authorities may control the time and place of a meeting.
rights.law: In re Ramlila Maidan Incident, Supreme Court, 23 February 2012, para 44 (Swatanter Kumar J.); (2012) 5 SCC 1
rights.quote: However, it must be borne in mind that the provisions of Section 144 Cr.P.C. are attracted only in emergent situations. The emergent power is to be exercised for the purposes of maintaining public order.

rights.title: What an unlawful assembly is
rights.point: A gathering of five or more people is an unlawful assembly only if they share one of a few aims the law lists. These are intimidating the government, a legislature or a public servant by criminal force or a show of it, resisting a law or legal process, committing mischief, criminal trespass or another offence, and using criminal force to take property or make someone act against their rights. A gathering that starts lawful can become unlawful later.
rights.law: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, section 189(1) and Explanation (replaces IPC section 141)
rights.quote: An assembly of five or more persons is designated an “unlawful assembly”, if the common object of the persons composing that assembly is— (a) to overawe by criminal force, or show of criminal force, the Central Government or any State Government ... (b) to resist the execution of any law, or of any legal process; or (c) to commit any mischief or criminal trespass, or other offence; ... Explanation.—An assembly which was not unlawful when it assembled, may subsequently become an unlawful assembly.

rights.title: Staying after an order to disperse
rights.point: Knowingly joining or staying in an unlawful assembly is punishable, and staying after it has been lawfully ordered to disperse carries a higher punishment. Staying in any gathering of five or more likely to disturb the peace after a lawful order to disperse is also an offence.
rights.law: BNS 2023, section 189(2), (3) and (5)
rights.quote: (3) Whoever joins or continues in an unlawful assembly, knowing that such unlawful assembly has been commanded in the manner prescribed by law to disperse, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

rights.title: Who can order a crowd to disperse
rights.point: An Executive Magistrate, the officer in charge of the police station or, in his absence, a police officer of at least sub-inspector rank can order an unlawful assembly, or a gathering of five or more likely to disturb the peace, to disperse. Its members then have a duty to leave, and if they do not, force may be used.
rights.law: BNSS 2023, section 148(1)-(2) (replaces CrPC section 129)
rights.quote: Any Executive Magistrate or officer in charge of a police station or, in the absence of such officer in charge, any police officer, not below the rank of a sub-inspector, may command any unlawful assembly, or any assembly of five or more persons likely to cause a disturbance of the public peace, to disperse; and it shall thereupon be the duty of the members of such assembly to disperse accordingly.

rights.title: Held without being arrested
rights.point: Everyone must follow the lawful directions a police officer gives while carrying out duties under the chapter of the Sanhita on preventive action by the police. A police officer may detain or remove a person who resists, refuses, ignores or disregards such a direction. The officer may then take the person before a magistrate or, in petty cases, release the person as soon as possible within twenty-four hours.
rights.law: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, section 172(1)-(2), in Chapter XII, 'Preventive action of the police'
rights.quote: 172. (1) All persons shall be bound to conform to the lawful directions of a police officer given in fulfilment of any of his duty under this Chapter. (2) A police officer may detain or remove any person resisting, refusing, ignoring or disregarding to conform to any direction given by him under sub-section (1) and may either take such person before a Magistrate or, in petty cases, release him as soon as possible within a period of twenty-four hours.

rights.title: Force must be minimal and proportionate
rights.point: The Supreme Court has said that police force is not warranted at all against a peaceful assembly. Where a crowd turns violent, reasonable force may be justified. The Court noted that police manuals and international covenants require force to be used only when it is absolutely necessary. When force is used, it should be the minimum needed and in proportion to the situation. It should stop as soon as the danger to life and property has passed.
rights.law: Anita Thakur v. Govt. of J&K, Supreme Court (A.K. Sikri and R.K. Agrawal JJ.), 12 August 2016, Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 118 of 2007, paras 12 and 13 (the judgment's own numbering, which Indian Kanoon shows)
rights.quote: 12. ... There are various documents in the form of police manual and even international covenants proscribing use of unnecessary force and mandating that force should only be used when it is absolutely necessary. Even when used, it should be minimum and proportional to the situation and its use to be discontinued as soon as the danger to life and property subsidised. 13. In those cases where assembly is peaceful, use of police force is not warranted at all. However, in those situations where crowd or assembly becomes violent it may necessitate and justify using reasonable police force.

rights.group: Where a protest may be held
rights.title: Protest areas cannot simply be banned
rights.point: The Supreme Court held that the authorities should regulate protests at Jantar Mantar and at the Boat Club in Delhi, and should not ban them altogether. It said the repeated prohibitory orders at the Boat Club amounted in practice to a ban, and directed the Delhi Police to frame guidelines, including prior permission, for limited use of both places.
rights.law: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India, Supreme Court, 23 July 2018, paras 63-65 (Jantar Mantar) and 69-70 (Boat Club); AIR 2018 SC 3476; (2018) 17 SCC 324
rights.quote: Though this analysis of the NGT is without blemish, we, however, feel that the solution was not to ban the demonstrations altogether. ... However, in reality no such activities are allowed at all and, therefore, the situation which is created amounts to ‘banning’ these public meetings, demonstrations, dharnas, etc. altogether rather than ‘regulating’ the same. 70) In the aforesaid conspectus, here also the Commissioner of Police, New Delhi and other official respondents can frame proper guidelines for regulating such protests, demonstrations, etc.

rights.group: Where a protest may be held
rights.title: Public roads cannot be occupied indefinitely
rights.point: The Supreme Court held that protesters cannot block a public road or occupy a public space indefinitely, and that protests must be held at designated places.
rights.law: Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police, Supreme Court, 7 October 2020, para 17 (AIR 2020 SC 4704)
rights.quote: we have to make it unequivocally clear that public ways and public spaces cannot be occupied in such a manner and that too indefinitely. Democracy and dissent go hand in hand, but then the demonstrations expressing dissent have to be in designated places alone.

rights.group: Where a protest may be held
rights.title: Permission rules vary by place
rights.point: Whether a protest needs police permission, and where it may be held, is set by local orders and differs from place to place. Ask at the local police station or a lawyer before the day.
rights.law: Example: the Delhi Police prohibitory orders, as read by the Supreme Court in Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018), para 68
rights.quote: The reading of these orders, thus, would indicate that there is no absolute prohibition from holding public meetings, processions, demonstrations, etc. Such activities are to be restricted in larger public interest and, therefore, before any group of persons or person wants to carry out any such processions and dharnas, it has to take prior written permission.

rights.title: Told why you are arrested
rights.point: If arrested, you must be told the grounds of arrest as soon as possible, and you can consult and be defended by a lawyer of your choice.
rights.law: Constitution of India, Article 22(1)
rights.quote: No person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest nor shall he be denied the right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of his choice.

rights.title: Before a magistrate within 24 hours
rights.point: You must be taken before a magistrate within 24 hours of arrest (not counting travel time), and cannot be held longer without the magistrate's order.
rights.law: Constitution of India, Article 22(2); BNSS 2023, sections 57 and 58
rights.quote: Every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the magistrate and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate.

rights.title: Full particulars of the offence, and bail
rights.point: Police arresting without a warrant must immediately tell you the full details of the offence. For a bailable offence they must tell you that you can be released on bail.
rights.law: BNSS 2023, section 47 (replaces CrPC section 50)
rights.quote: (1) Every police officer or other person arresting any person without warrant shall forthwith communicate to him full particulars of the offence for which he is arrested or other grounds for such arrest. (2) Where a police officer arrests without warrant any person other than a person accused of a non-bailable offence, he shall inform the person arrested that he is entitled to be released on bail and that he may arrange for sureties on his behalf.

rights.title: Someone you name must be told
rights.point: The police must at once tell a relative, friend or other person you name that you have been arrested and where you are being held, and tell you of this right at the police station.
rights.law: BNSS 2023, section 48(1)-(2) (replaces CrPC section 50A)
rights.quote: Every police officer or other person making any arrest under this Sanhita shall forthwith give the information regarding such arrest and place where the arrested person is being held to any of his relatives, friends or such other persons as may be disclosed or nominated by the arrested person for the purpose of giving such information and also to the designated police officer in the district.

rights.title: Officer identification and arrest memo
rights.point: The arresting officer must wear a clear name identification and prepare an arrest memo, witnessed by a family member or a respectable local person and signed by you.
rights.law: BNSS 2023, section 36 (replaces CrPC section 41B); D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal, (1997) 1 SCC 416, decided 18 December 1996, requirements (1)-(2)
rights.quote: Every police officer while making an arrest shall— (a) bear an accurate, visible and clear identification of his name which will facilitate easy identification; (b) prepare a memorandum of arrest which shall be— (i) attested by at least one witness, who is a member of the family of the person arrested or a respectable member of the locality where the arrest is made; (ii) countersigned by the person arrested; and (c) inform the person arrested, unless the memorandum is attested by a member of his family, that he has a right to have a relative or a friend or any other person named by him to be informed of his arrest.

rights.title: Meeting a lawyer during questioning
rights.point: You may meet a lawyer of your choice during police questioning, though not for the whole of it.
rights.law: BNSS 2023, section 38 (replaces CrPC section 41D); D.K. Basu requirement (10)
rights.quote: When any person is arrested and interrogated by the police, he shall be entitled to meet an advocate of his choice during interrogation, though not throughout interrogation.

rights.title: Notice to appear instead of arrest
rights.point: If the police do not need to arrest you, they must instead give you a notice to appear before them, and you must comply with it. If you comply, you should not be arrested for that offence unless the officer records reasons. If you do not comply, or will not identify yourself, you can be arrested.
rights.law: BNSS 2023, section 35(3)-(6) (replaces CrPC section 41A)
rights.quote: (3) The police officer shall, in all cases where the arrest of a person is not required under sub-section (1) issue a notice directing the person against whom a reasonable complaint has been made, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists that he has committed a cognizable offence, to appear before him or at such other place as may be specified in the notice. ... (5) Where such person complies and continues to comply with the notice, he shall not be arrested in respect of the offence referred to in the notice unless, for reasons to be recorded, the police officer is of the opinion that he ought to be arrested.

rights.title: Medical examination
rights.point: After arrest you must be examined by a government medical officer, or a registered medical practitioner if none is available, soon after the arrest.
rights.law: BNSS 2023, section 53(1) (replaces CrPC section 54)
rights.quote: When any person is arrested, he shall be examined by a medical officer in the service of the Central Government or a State Government, and in case the medical officer is not available, by a registered medical practitioner soon after the arrest is made:

rights.title: Grounds of arrest in writing
rights.point: The Supreme Court has held that a person arrested for any offence, under any law including the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, must be given the grounds of arrest in writing, in a language they understand. If the officer cannot give them in writing at the time of arrest or soon after, the grounds must be told to the person orally. They must then be given in writing within a reasonable time, and at least two hours before the person is produced before the magistrate for remand. If this is not done, the arrest and the remand that follows are illegal and the person is free to go. The police may then ask the magistrate for custody again, giving their reasons, but only after giving the grounds in writing and explaining why they were not given in time. The Court said this procedure governs arrests from its judgment of 6 November 2025 onwards.
rights.law: Mihir Rajesh Shah v. State of Maharashtra, Supreme Court (B.R. Gavai CJI and Augustine George Masih J.), 6 November 2025, Criminal Appeal No. 2195 of 2025, (2026) 1 SCC 500; paras 55, 56 and 58 in the judgment's own numbering as printed and shown on Indian Kanoon (paras 65, 66 and 68 in the SCC report, as Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol v. State of Punjab, 21 September 2026, para 24, cites them)
rights.quote: 55. It goes without saying that if the abovesaid schedule for supplying the grounds of arrest in writing is not adhered to, the arrest will be rendered illegal entitling the release of the arrestee. On such release, an application for remand or custody, if required, will be moved along with the reasons and necessity for the same, after the supply of the grounds of arrest in writing setting forth the explanation for non-supply thereof within the above stipulated schedule. 56. In conclusion, it is held that: i) The constitutional mandate of informing the arrestee the grounds of arrest is mandatory in all offences under all statutes including offences under IPC 1860 (now BNS 2023); ii) The grounds of arrest must be communicated in writing to the arrestee in the language he/she understands; iii) In case(s) where, the arresting officer/person is unable to communicate the grounds of arrest in writing on or soon after arrest, it be so done orally. The said grounds be communicated in writing within a reasonable time and in any case at least two hours prior to production of the arrestee for remand proceedings before the magistrate. iv) In case of non-compliance of the above, the arrest and subsequent remand would be rendered illegal and the person will be at liberty to be set free. ... 58. ... The ends of fairness and legal discipline therefore demand that this procedure as affirmed above shall govern arrests henceforth.

rights.title: The right to stay silent
rights.point: No one accused of an offence can be forced to be a witness against themselves. A person the police question during an investigation must answer truthfully the questions about the case. The law excuses that person from answering questions whose answers would tend to expose them to a criminal charge, a penalty or forfeiture.
rights.law: Constitution of India, Article 20(3); Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, section 180(1)-(2) (replaces CrPC section 161)
rights.quote: Article 20(3): "No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself." BNSS section 180: "(1) Any police officer making an investigation under this Chapter ... may examine orally any person supposed to be acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case. (2) Such person shall be bound to answer truly all questions relating to such case put to him by such officer, other than questions the answers to which would have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge or to a penalty or forfeiture."

rights.title: Disobeying an order needs a public servant's complaint before a court can act
rights.point: A court cannot take up an offence under sections 206 to 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, except section 209, unless the public servant concerned complains in writing. The complaint can also come from that public servant's superior, or from a public servant they have authorised. These sections include obstructing a public servant (section 221) and disobeying an order made by a public servant (section 223). The rule stops a court from taking cognizance of the offence. Its words do not stop the police from registering a case.
rights.law: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, section 215(1)(a) (replaces CrPC section 195(1)(a))
rights.quote: 215. (1) No Court shall take cognizance— (a) (i) of any offence punishable under sections 206 to 223 (both inclusive but excluding section 209) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; or (ii) of any abetment of, or attempt to commit, such offence; or (iii) of any criminal conspiracy to commit such offence, except on the complaint in writing of the public servant concerned or of some other public servant to whom he is administratively subordinate or of some other public servant who is authorised by the concerned public servant so to do;

rights.title: Obstructing a public servant (s.221 BNS)
rights.point: Voluntarily obstructing a public servant in carrying out public functions is punishable with up to three months in prison, a fine of up to 2,500 rupees, or both. The offence is non-cognizable and bailable. For this offence alone, the police cannot arrest without a warrant and cannot investigate without a magistrate's order. A case that also includes a cognizable offence is treated as a cognizable case as a whole.
rights.law: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, section 221 (replaces IPC section 186); BNSS 2023, First Schedule, Part I, row for section 221, and Explanatory Note (2); BNSS section 174(2) and (4)
rights.quote: BNS 221: "Whoever voluntarily obstructs any public servant in the discharge of his public functions, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to two thousand and five hundred rupees, or with both." BNSS First Schedule: "221 | Obstructing public servant in discharge of his public functions. | Imprisonment for 3 months, or fine of 2,500 rupees, or both. | Non-cognizable. | Bailable. | Any Magistrate." Explanatory Note (2): "the word "non-cognizable" stands for "a police officer shall not arrest without warrant"". BNSS 174: "(2) No police officer shall investigate a non-cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate having power to try such case or commit the case for trial. ... (4) Where a case relates to two or more offences of which at least one is cognizable, the case shall be deemed to be a cognizable case, notwithstanding that the other offences are non-cognizable."

rights.title: Obstructing police dispersing an assembly (s.195 BNS)
rights.point: Assaulting or obstructing a public servant, or using criminal force on one, while the public servant is trying to disperse an unlawful assembly or put down a riot or affray, is punishable with up to three years in prison, a fine of at least 25,000 rupees, or both. The offence is cognizable and bailable.
rights.law: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, section 195(1) (replaces IPC section 152); BNSS 2023, First Schedule, Part I, row for section 195(1)
rights.quote: BNS 195: "(1) Whoever assaults or obstructs any public servant or uses criminal force on any public servant in the discharge of his duty as such public servant in endeavouring to disperse an unlawful assembly, or to suppress a riot or affray, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which shall not be less than twenty-five thousand rupees, or with both." BNSS First Schedule: "195(1) | Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc. | Imprisonment for 3 years, or fine not less than 25,000 rupees, or both. | Cognizable. | Bailable. | Magistrate of the first class."

rights.title: Assault or force to deter a public servant (s.132 BNS)
rights.point: Assaulting or using criminal force on a public servant who is carrying out their duty, or to stop them doing it, or because of something they did lawfully in that duty, is punishable with up to two years in prison, a fine, or both. The offence is cognizable and non-bailable. A person accused of a non-bailable offence may still be released on bail, but has no right to it, and the police officer or court decides.
rights.law: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, section 132 (replaces IPC section 353); BNSS 2023, First Schedule, Part I, row for section 132; BNSS section 480(1)
rights.quote: BNS 132: "Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person being a public servant in the execution of his duty as such public servant, or with intent to prevent or deter that person from discharging his duty as such public servant, or in consequence of anything done or attempted to be done by such person in the lawful discharge of his duty as such public servant, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both." BNSS First Schedule: "132 | Assault or use of criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty. | Imprisonment for 2 years, or fine, or both. | Cognizable. | Non-bailable. | Any Magistrate." BNSS 480: "(1) When any person accused of, or suspected of, the commission of any non-bailable offence is arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police station or appears or is brought before a Court other than the High Court or Court of Session, he may be released on bail, but—"

rights.title: Women: no arrest at night, save exceptionally
rights.point: A woman should not be arrested after sunset and before sunrise, except in exceptional circumstances. In such a case a woman police officer must first make a written report and get the permission of a first-class Magistrate.
rights.law: BNSS 2023, section 43(5) (replaces CrPC section 46(4))
rights.quote: (5) Save in exceptional circumstances, no woman shall be arrested after sunset and before sunrise, and where such exceptional circumstances exist, the woman police officer shall, by making a written report, obtain the prior permission of the Magistrate of the first class within whose local jurisdiction the offence is committed or the arrest is to be made.

rights.title: Women: not to be touched by a male officer
rights.point: When a woman is arrested, she is presumed to submit to custody once told orally of the arrest, unless the circumstances suggest otherwise, and a male officer should not touch her to make the arrest unless the circumstances require it. When a woman has to be searched, the search must be made by another woman, with strict regard to decency.
rights.law: BNSS 2023, section 43(1) proviso; section 49(2)
rights.quote: Provided that where a woman is to be arrested, unless the circumstances indicate to the contrary, her submission to custody on an oral intimation of arrest shall be presumed and, unless the circumstances otherwise require or unless the police officer is a female, the police officer shall not touch the person of the woman for making her arrest.

rights.title: Children
rights.point: When the police apprehend a child alleged to have committed an offence, the child must be placed in the charge of the special juvenile police unit or the designated child welfare police officer. That officer must bring the child before the Juvenile Justice Board without delay, and within twenty-four hours of apprehending the child, leaving out the time needed for the journey. A child alleged to have committed an offence must never be placed in a police lockup or lodged in a jail.
rights.law: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, section 10(1) and proviso
rights.quote: 10. (1) As soon as a child alleged to be in conflict with law is apprehended by the police, such child shall be placed under the charge of the special juvenile police unit or the designated child welfare police officer, who shall produce the child before the Board without any loss of time but within a period of twenty-four hours of apprehending the child excluding the time necessary for the journey, from the place where such child was apprehended: Provided that in no case, a child alleged to be in conflict with law shall be placed in a police lockup or lodged in a jail.

rights.group: Complaining about force used by police
rights.title: Complaining about force used by police
rights.point: If the officer in charge of a police station refuses to record information about a cognizable offence, the person can send the substance of it in writing and by post to the Superintendent of Police. If that officer does not act on it, the person can apply to a magistrate, and the application must be supported by an affidavit. Where the complaint is against a public servant over something that arose in the course of official duties, the magistrate may order an investigation after receiving a report on the incident from that officer's superior. The magistrate must also consider the public servant's own account of what led to the incident.
rights.law: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, section 173(4) (replaces CrPC section 154(3)); section 175(3) (replaces CrPC section 156(3)); section 175(4) (new, with no counterpart in the CrPC)
rights.quote: Section 173(4): "Any person aggrieved by a refusal on the part of an officer in charge of a police station to record the information referred to in sub-section (1), may send the substance of such information, in writing and by post, to the Superintendent of Police concerned who, if satisfied that such information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence, shall either investigate the case himself or direct an investigation to be made by any police officer subordinate to him ... failing which such aggrieved person may make an application to the Magistrate." Section 175: "(3) Any Magistrate empowered under section 210 may, after considering the application supported by an affidavit made under sub-section (4) of section 173, and after making such inquiry as he thinks necessary and submission made in this regard by the police officer, order such an investigation as above-mentioned. (4) Any Magistrate empowered under section 210, may, upon receiving a complaint against a public servant arising in course of the discharge of his official duties, order investigation, subject to— (a) receiving a report containing facts and circumstances of the incident from the officer superior to him; and (b) after consideration of the assertions made by the public servant as to the situation that led to the incident so alleged."

rights.title: Free legal aid: the Constitution
rights.point: The Constitution directs the State to provide free legal aid so that nobody is denied justice because they are poor or disadvantaged.
rights.law: Constitution of India, Article 39A
rights.quote: The State shall secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice, on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall, in particular, provide free legal aid, by suitable legislation or schemes or in any other way, to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.

rights.title: Free legal aid: who qualifies
rights.point: If you have a case to bring or defend, you are entitled to free legal services if you belong to one of the groups the law lists. These include anyone in custody, women and children, members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, persons with disabilities, victims of trafficking or of a disaster, ethnic violence or caste atrocity, industrial workers, and anyone earning below the income limit their state sets. The legal services authority must be satisfied that you have a prima facie case, and a sworn statement of your income is normally enough.
rights.law: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, sections 12 and 13
rights.quote: Every person who has to file or defend a case shall be entitled to legal services under this Act if that person is — (a) a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe; ... (c) a woman or a child; ... (g) in custody, ...
